SUGGESTED INTRODUCTION OF LEGISLATION TO COMPEL PROFESSIONAL LEAGUES TO CONTRIBUTE TO THE DEVELOPMENT OF TALENT-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the provisions of Standing Order 43 I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity. In view of the fact that yesterday the Minister of State (Fitness and Amateur Sport) said that the government had failed in trying to mediate a truce between major junior hockey teams and professional leagues regarding the payment of development fees because "the federal government has neither the legislation nor the jurisdiction to resolve the dispute", and since this same government has in fact established a precedent in introducing legislation dealing specifically with professional sports, namely by intervening in professional football, for the sake of preserving a healthy continuation of our national sport as well as the development of other amateur participation I move, seconded by the hon. member for Edmonton Centre (Mr. Paproski):
That this House instruct the Minister of State responsible for sports to take all necessary steps for legislation to be introduced whereby all professional teams, leagues or shows, including the NHL and WHA, contribute realistically toward the development of their respective sports, in accordance with such legislation.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR LOANS TO MUNICIPALITIES AT COST OF ADMINISTRATION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to the terms of Standing Order 43, I request the unanimous consent of the House to present a motion for the discussion of an urgent and important matter.
As most municipal administrations are now having tremendous difficulties in paying back their debts, which results, on the one hand, in making it very difficult for them to borrow money on which they have to pay 13 and 14 per cent interest, without increasing their taxes and, on the other hand, in making it impossible for them to meet their expenses; as there is an imbalance between their income and their needs because land and property taxes, their sole source of income, are really inadequate to meet their financial responsibilities; and also because the interest on their public debt affects greatly their respective budgets; and also because municipal governments are the very foundation of our democratic system and, as a consequence, are the level of the government which is closest to the citizens, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Richmond (Mr. Beaudoin):
That this House order the government, and through it the Bank of Canada, to authorize loans to municipalities, at cost, so that they can finance non-profitable public development projects such as hospitals, schools, roads, etc.; and this, to enable municipal administrations to reduce their debts and meet their needs adequately.

subsubtopic: AMENDMENT TO INCREASE SUBSCRIPTION TO INTERNATIONAL MONETARY FUND AND INTERNATIONAL BANK FOR CONSTRUCTION AND DEVELOPMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on Bill C-18, an act to amend the Bretton Woods Agreements Act, let me say that I believe it is salutary at this time to discuss the international financial situation, particularly as the whole thrust of the Bretton Woods Agreement has changed over the years so that now we are called upon to deal primarily with underdeveloped countries demanding loans and financial support, which was certainly not conceived of when the first Bretton Woods Agreement was achieved.
I think it is wise to take a look at what was the purpose of the 1944 Bretton Woods Agreement. It was to keep different currencies of the world in a stable relationship with one another and to provide loans with which the war devastated countries could finance their reconstruction and future development. The representatives at that time drew up plans for a fund with which to stabilize currencies, and for a bank to make loans. The fund was to be an international monetary fund to be made up of deposits of currencies, of gold, and of securities of all member nations. This $9 billion fund was to be divided among the nations in accordance with the size and wealth of the various countries making contributions. The fund was to be used by nations when needed, and a comprehensive set of rules was worked out according to which the fund was to be put to use.
The second proposal of the International Bank for Construction and Development was to set up a $10 billion capital which was to be funded from the purchase of shares by various nations in accordance with their ability. The bank was to lend money to governments and to guarantee private loans to them in order that reconstruction of the devastated countries and the development of the less advanced countries could be facilitated. The purpose of the fund was to keep world currencies in a
Bretton Woods Agreements
stable relationship with one and other and thus to stabilize world trade.
The International Monetary Fund has been of considerable value. It is a currency pool into which member countries may dip when they are short of foreign currencies. Amounts which a needy country can take out are limited to the amount which the country has put into it.
The International Development Bank is somewhat different in that it has become a borrower of last resort. When a government or a private firm is unable to borrow on its own resources, the IDB steps into the breach.
Since 1944 the whole character of the economic problems facing the world has changed. War ravaged Europe and the Far East have been reconstructed. Germany and Japan, the defeated nations, have become extremely strong, even stronger in many ways than the U.S.A. which was the original main contributor to the Bretton Woods Agreement. These two countries are now involved in providing equitable and financial aid to underdeveloped countries and in rectifying the weaknesses of the key currency systems. These developments have changed the direction of the Bretton Woods Agreement. The introduction of the Special Drawing Rights by the IMF was designed to supplement and supply the other components of international resources, such as gold and U.S. dollar liabilities, but in effect the Special Drawing Rights really increase the liquidity of the entire international monetary system. They are no more like owned reserves than borrowed reserves.
The problem with the SDR scheme is to determine the amount of SDRs to be created. The proposal is that the IMF play an important role in resolving these conflicts through the creation of further allotments of SDRs. It is to do this through the managing director of the IMF after consultation with members who would recommend the amount of SDRs to be created.
The United States and the bloc of Common Market countries will have effective veto power because 85 per cent of the affirmative vote by the board of governors of the IMF is required to ratify the managing director's recommendation. It is to be hoped that this new departure will allow the IMF to continue to play a stabilizing role in the evolution of the fund. Some of the advantages of the fund, it has been argued, are that it has enabled an international monetary system to evolve in a number of different ways, including the deliberate creation of SDRs and increased co-operation amongst central banks. However, the fund seems to have been much less successful in dealing with the exchange rate problems and techniques of adjustment.
The World Bank has introduced two agencies, the IDA and the International Financial Corporation. The IDA was formed in 1960 to provide very soft loans to the poorest of the less developed countries. This was to reduce the strain of payment, and loans were on a 50 year basis. However, the funds were certainly small and did not cover the small loans needs of underdeveloped countries. The International Financial Corporation was to provide venture capital to the private sector of
80016-35'/2

May 25, 1977
Bretton Woods Agreements
the economy, and private companies were to assume control as soon as possible.
The international monetary system did not evolve as was foreseen by the architects of the Bretton Woods Agreement. Perhaps keeping in mind the disasters of the thirties, they considered that gains from the international trade integration would be far greater than from those of international financial integration, and therefore allowed controls on capital flows as opposed to merchandise flows, a situation which, incidentally, we are approaching now with our demands for trade controls. This increase in international trade has created a demand for payment which has largely been met by the American dollar. An extensive international credit system has evolved so that the American dollar has emerged as the vehicle currency of the world. As might be expected, this dominance of the American dollar has not met with uniform acceptance. Many countries have objected to this extension of the American dollar.
In any case, in the foreseeable future the American dollar will be extremely dominant. It will have the effect of being a sort of world currency. Some would argue for this; that the United States would have to give up a large part of its domestic power; and that American monetary policy would have to be in tune to international needs rather than to American needs.
This brings up the role of the United States in the world, that of the other developed countries of the west and their relationship with the Third World. The debate is now proceeding. Over the past 20 years the western world has given in increasingly to the idea that, at all costs, Third World needs must be supplied. Some have the idea that the standard of living in black Africa is low because the standard of living in the western world is high. It has always interested me that, in our discussions of our obligations to underdeveloped countries, while the western world must give money, services and goods, the communist world is not called on to give anything, and indeed, it usually gives soldiers and guns to foment revolution.
President Jimmy Carter was quoted in yesterday's Globe and Mail as saying the following:
Our policy must reflect our belief that the world can hope for more than simple survival and must help shape an international system that will last longer than secret deals.
We are now free of that inordinate fear of communism.
It is difficult to feel that we do not need to be afraid of communism, particularly when the Russian navy is immense, when our own Admiral Boyle has suggested there could well be a war with the communists by 1980, and when no one has disputed the enormous building up of Soviet military power. This certainly makes one realize that communism is certainly still a force in the world.
President Carter also seemed to feel that there was decreasing importance in the United Nations, the North Atlantic Treaty Organization and the World Bank, which he felt had been part of an international system which had worked well

for a quarter of a century. However, I thought he added other significantly desirable policy solutions. President Carter also said:
That system could not last forever unchanged. Historical trends have weakened its foundation. The unifying threat of conflict with the Soviet Union has become less intensive, even though the competition has become more extensive.
President Carter went on to say:
It is no longer possible to separate the issues of war and peace from those of justice and human rights.
We can no longer have a policy solely for the industrial nations as the foundation of global stability, but we must respond to the new reality of a politically awakening world .. .
Now, the policy must close the gap between rich and poor nations and encourage all countries to rise above narrow national interest and work to resolve the formidable problems facing the world.
The speech of the President of the United States seems to be an attempt to seek further compromises with the world, to reaffirm U.S. commitments to human rights and, in effect, to qualify support for Israel after the recent election of the right wing Likud coalition, whose leader, Mr. Begin, has taken a harder line with the Arab world.
President Carter seems also to have written off southern Africa, so it may come under the domination of the left wing world. We can, however, applaud this statement by President Carter:
We know that a peaceful world cannot exist one third rich and two thirds hungry.
However, it is doubtful that a peaceful world will come about easily.
Because most of the debate on the role of Third World countries will take place in the United States, it seems important that we know what is happening in the United States. The oil embargo of March, 1974, rudely brought home to the Americans the power of the Third World, and the public debate on the new international economic order takes place when the U.S. public is more aware of the Third World than it ever was previously.
As usual, in a debate such as this there are two broad positions. One tends to accommodate the Third World, and the other tends towards resistance. Soft liners argue for accommodation on the grounds of both expediency and justice, whereas hardliners contest the argument on the same grounds. Softlin-ers, looking ahead, perceive an increasingly interdependent world in which there must be a new order which takes cognizance of the interests of all nations, including the poor ones. However, many question the optimistic consequences of the softliners. In the minds of many, interdependence is likely to diminish conflicts. The opposite is more probable. An example might even be found in our own country. The modern world has brought about more interdependence, but we have become more disunited. Interdependence in itself is not conducive to order. Rather, power, political and military, has been the foundation of order both within and between nations.
Softliners promote the view that the interdependent nations of the west are very vulnerable to disruptions by less developed nations, and therefore it is in the interests of the interdepend-
May 25, 1977

ent nations to adopt a policy of accommodation. The hardliners would argue that power is as important as it has ever been, and certainly the Russian and Cuban expansions in Africa have been based on the use of power. In recent years the western nations have been unwilling to employ their power, which makes interdependence so vulnerable.
Furthermore, there are two different viewpoints on egalitarianism in the world. Third World countries, nearly all dictatorships, are interested in greater equality amongst states. The western elitists, enamoured of the new egalitarianism, are thinking of the equality of individuals. In other words, the moral appeal of the new international economic order is based on a confusion between domestic and international realities. 1 suggest there is a profound difference between equality between states and equality between individuals.
There is no real evidence that giving in to Third World demands will have the effect of toning the Third World down. Indeed, policies of accommodation are likely to whet appetites. Nor does it seem to be true that either greater equality or greater order among nations would be the likely outcome even if the entire world became a system of socialist states.
There are probably two credible views of the way ahead. The world could be a much more disorderly place or, more likely, a new power similar to the Roman Empire, the Great Britain of Victorian times or the United States of the last 25 years could emerge. The Soviet Union appears to be a likely candidate for that role.
I do not believe we should give some kind of reparation to the Third World because of past or present exploitation. Certainly western imperialism has bestowed a period of economic and social benefits on the Third World.
To me there are other aspects of this problem which those who want to give large amounts of aid to the Third World have not adequately considered. The fundamental problem of most Third World countries has not been that they have not been able to increase their output of goods and services but that the burgeoning birth rate has meant the increase in goods and services has been eaten up, and so the individual is no better off than before. While control of the birth rate seems possible some way ahead, it shows little sign of making much of a dent in the immediate future.
The transfer of vast amounts of aid from the western world may well prop up the nation states such as the one headed by Idi Amin, but it does not do much to aid the individual citizen. In the future will we remain-"we" being Canadians as well as Americans-unmoved by mass starvation shown on our evening television news? Can we find a middle road that will not be hard-hearted but will be morally sensitive without being sentimental?
I am glad to have had this opportunity to say a few things on the Bretton Woods Agreement and the way ahead, dealing particularly with the Third World which I think is very important to Canadians as a whole.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a few short remarks on this bill. What disturbs me most is that it is being put forth and its quick passage sought by the same people who have given us record inflation, record unemployment, record trade deficits, record budget deficits, record bank interest rates, record mortgage rates, record high energy prices, the highest level of foreign borrowing of any western nation, low productivity, the highest cost of government in our history, the worst track record in recent history, the Sky Shops affair, dredging scandals-this bill is put forward by a government that has no discernible energy policy, no discernible foreign policy, and no discernible industrial strategy.
This same government is negotiating in secret at the GATT conference. This bill is put forward by a government that has no known targets that we can see regarding the money supply, and no national objectives for industrial growth other than the reference by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Mac-Eachen) in this House recently when he said he hoped some of the growth in the United States economy would splash over the border and spur on our economy. I think that is a deplorable record for any government.
In presenting this bill the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) said, as reported at page 5888 of Hansard:
According to Article I of its articles of agreement, the fund is charged with facilitating the expansion and growth of world trade and payments as a means of raising world standards of living and of fostering economic development.
I think it is obvious to everyone that the government is in violation of Article I of the International Monetary Fund articles on its own domestic policy. How can we sit on international boards and committees and talk about the expansion of world trade while our share of trade is shrinking? How can we be perceived as a credible nation when there is so much disorder within the Canadian economy? How can the government be perceived to be serious about expanded world trade when it is negotiating with GATT in secret? How can our industries expand when they simply do not know what is going on at the GATT conference in Geneva? How can we continue to assist the Third World countries when inflation in this country is continuing to sap our vitality and growth?
If you look at the growth of the money supply in Canada over the past 15 years there is one real lesson: with moderate monetary growth there was no inflation in Canada, with the expansion of monetary growth there was a relatively mild inflation, when the growth rate fell inflation fell, and when the monetary growth rate reached the sky, of course we had double-digit inflation.
The Bank of Canada Act in Section 14.(2) reads as follows:
(2) If, notwithstanding the consultations provided for in subsection (1), there should emerge a difference of opinion between the Minister and .the Bank concerning the monetary policy to be followed, the Minister may, after consultation with the Governor and with the approval of the Governor in Council, give to the Governor a written directive concerning monetary policy, in specific terms and applicable for a specified period, and the Bank shall comply with such directive.
What I am saying is that we cannot slough off this matter of growth of money supply on the Governor of the Bank of

May 25, 1977
Bretton Woods Agreements
Canada; it falls on the incumbent minister of finance and the cabinet.
Speaking in Halifax in 1975 the Governor of the Bank of Canada said:
If the ultimate goal-the restoration of a completely stable price level, that is zero rate of inflation-is to be achieved, this will eventually require the maintenance of an average rate of growth of the money supply no higher than the long-term average rate of growth of the production of goods and services in Canada-that is a rate of about 5 per cent a year.
Bill C-18 merely broadens the base. It is similar to a businessman who finds himself at the limit of his line of credit while running his business at a loss. Instead of putting his house in order and effecting a turn-around, to a break even and a profit position, he merely gets a further extension in his line of credit and pushes the inevitable consequences into the future.
Had the minister come to this House, as he could have, at the time of his budget and announced a set of economic goals, a target date for a balanced budget, and a disciplined step-bystep monetary policy, then we could have looked at Bill C-18 in a different context.
It is well known that we have a record balance of payments deficit. Balance of payments deficits may be removed by internal economic and industrial policies, or financed by borrowings. The government has chosen the latter route and has mortgaged the country so far into the future that it is frightening.
Deficit financing by borrowings is not a practicable way to stabilize an economy over a long period of time. In the last nine years we have had one surplus and eight deficit budgets. Surely it is evident to the minister and his officials that they are on the wrong track. Through their taxation policies they have taken away the ability of the people of this country to accumulate wealth that is expressed eventually in investment in industrial growth. Lacking industrial growth we are now on a course toward lower tariffs that will further distort our balance of payments deficit.
The realities of our financial problem are evidenced in the flight of investment money from Canada. The outflow in 1976 exceeds the inflow of funds by $1 billion. Our financial plight is continually clouded by over-playing internal social policies. You simply cannot pursue gradual monetary goals when overall confidence in the economy is lacking. When you tighten the money supply the difference can be taken up by the velocity of the money already in circulation. This will only occur when there is confidence in the economy.
We are not really happy with this bill, Mr. Speaker. We are not happy with the government and its inability to deal with the economy of Canada. If we continue on our present course, Canada will be numbered among the Third World countries and be a net recipient of aid from others. We do not have to accept inflation. If we want to help Third World countries, we should do it by encouraging them to be self-reliant. If we are to do that, we must become more self-reliant in this country.

The tasks confronting all governments of the western world surely are these: assuring stable growth, maintaining full employment, avoiding inflation, keeping the balance of payments in equilibrium, and maintaining the integrity of national currency. Those are some main objectives. The government has failed miserably to meet these vital objectives, and the evidence of its failure is apparent.
When this bill is considered in committee we shall question the minister and the officials. That the economy of Canada is being handled so badly is tragic. The minister has had numerous opportunities to introduce fiscal and monetary policies which would improve our position in the world. Today we face the prospect of a Canadian dollar dropping in value. I hope it will not happen, but if the views of many pessimists in the money markets prevail, the Canadian dollar will drop a considerable amount in the next few months. I hope it will not happen, but the signs that it will are there to be seen. I do not think the agreements we are debating will do much to stop that trend. We are part of the western world, are considered a developed country, and must support agreements of this kind. If we are to play a significant role in the world economy, the government must accept the challenge confronting it and act with urgency.

ny Boeckh. The hon. member contended that we ought to run this country in accordance with the kinds of statistics and tables economists of that kind have prepared. With one million Canadians out of work, boy oh boy, where is your heart?

There is the voice of ignorance and stupidity over there, again.
I should like to direct attention to the constructive remarks made by the hon. member for Edmonton-Strathcona (Mr. Roche). He talked on the question of transferring funds to the developing world and the problems of liquidity which less developed countries are encountering as a result of the worldwide increase in energy prices. As I said yesterday, in many cases it is as a result of the drop in export prices of primary exports from these countries. The hon. member asked me to make some comment on the possibility of linking the further creation of Special Drawing Rights with special discriminatory advantages in favour of the developing countries. Probably we would have to take some disagreement with that as an approach.
Contrary to what the hon. member says, the IMF is not truly a central bank, although it is true that there are some similarities in their functions. It is also true to say that the SDR is a form of international money. We have supported the increase of the SDR. It is gradually taking the position as the central element in the international monetary system. However, we think that proposals to link future SDR allocations to direct income redistribution to LDCs would be counter-productive. The goal of making SDRs the central monetary asset would be undermined and the LDCs would likely not receive any net increase in resources from the developed world.
The hon. member also talked of the role of the World Bank and of the IMF. I should emphasize again the distinction in function between these two organizations. The IMF has the responsibility basically for the short-term balance of payments problems of members, both developed and developing countries. The World Bank has been responsible primarily for financing developing countries and development in the de-

veloping world. In this regard, through its two subsidiaries, the International Development Association and the International Finance Corporation, the World Bank has already extended in the case of IDA grant assistance to the developing world, and in the case of IFC assistance to equity investment in the same area.
One of the difficulties we have recently talked about in international forums has been the immediate balance of payments problem. In this regard the managing director of the International Monetary Fund, Mr. Witteveen, has come up with some proposals with regard to helping to meet the short-term balance of payment problems of many other countries. His efforts with regard to establishing the so-called Witteveen facility have been very progressive efforts.
It is very useful that the OPEC countries-Saudi Arabia, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates-have offered to come forward along with developed countries for the purpose of establishing this additional fund. However, I do not think either the countries involved or this House should lose sight of the fact that the facility is at best a temporary financing solution and that both the OPEC countries and the developed world must continue to assist on an increasing scale the developing countries through official development assistance.
Over the long run, funds drawn out of the Witteveen facility will have to be paid back. They can only be paid back if official development assistance continues to flow into those countries, making it possible for them to meet these other obligations.
There were a number of points raised by other members. They could more effectively be dealt with in detail before the committee. I would say again that with the officials we would be quite prepared to discuss in detail both the operation of the proposed amendments to the International Monetary Fund and take the occasion at the same time to talk about amendments to the Currency and Exchange Fund Act, the Canadian and domestic legislation, and also to discuss forthcoming policy with regard to the continuing financing of balance of payments problem, both in the developed and developing world.
Is the House ready for the question?

speechtext:
that Bill C-46, to amend the Aeronautics Act and the National Trans-
May 25, 1977

portation Act, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.
He said: Mr. Speaker, this is a short but important bill. It raises several fairly narrow questions. I will be quite brief in dealing with it.
The purpose of the bill is to deal with the issue that arose after the Supreme Court decision in connection with some issues before it arising out of the purchase by the Alberta government of Pacific Western Airlines. The Supreme Court in particular dealt with the issue of the Crown in right of the province and its obligations in relation to the general regulatory framework over which the Canadian Transport Commissi-son has jurisdiction.
The finding that Her Majesty in the right of a province was not properly before or bound by the regulatory framework, raised for us immediately the question of changing the law in that regard. It seems a fairly obvious proposition that it would defeat the broad overview which the Canadian Transport Commission and similar administrative agencies must have over a transportation function if important aspects of that function in interprovincial and international transportation particularly were not within the ambit of regulations.
The bill before us changes the situation. It makes it clear that the Aeronautics Act is indeed binding on Her Majesty in right of Canada or a province or an agent of either one of them. That is the simplest legal change being made.
In addition, there are changes being made which provide for certain procedures to be followed in the event that such interests or involvements are in fact undertaken by provinces or their agents. It is implicit in the policy in the bill that it may be generally unwise to have a provincial government in ownership of a body controlling transportation which is federally regulated, particularly if that transportation is interprovincial or international in its nature.
The problems which arise are essentially two. The first is the problem for the administrative tribunal if it is dealing with an applicant which is essentially a provincial government. This arises from the fact that while a province may hereby be made a person, it really will not be a person like other persons which may be involved in transportation. Indeed, the question arises of whether a controversy may arise or rage about an administrative tribunal in a way which would endanger its over-all jurisdiction and responsibilities.
Second, there is the problem that in interprovincial services, and indeed in international ones, certain issues may arise where the provincial interest may be in conflict with the provision of service to other provinces also being provided with service by the entity in question. There the question of fairness may be very difficult to assess. It may therefore be better to leave the position where generally a province is not in a position of ownership. I use the word generally because of the fact that certain circumstances may arise where a particular operation does not give rise to these considerations.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I shall not be too long, particularly since the minister has now indicated clearly with respect to this bill, which does correct certain oversights which are of some concern to all of us in this Chamber with respect to the rights of the provinces to act outside of or independent of certain regulations set down by agencies which are in fact integral parts of the federal government structure and which are designed to maintain some order and some discipline not only in the air industry but in other industries as well, that we can all anticipate other amendments similar to this with respect to other modes of transport and other areas of activity which fall within the ambit of the federal regulatory authority. In fact the government has moved in the right direction today to correct an oversight.
All of which is to say that I do not think there was in the minds of any of us any intent to be critical or to suggest that the province of Alberta in moving into this very vital area of transport had intended anything untoward with respect to the regulatory agencies.
If I understand correctly, the minister intends at a later stage to introduce an amendment which would permit extension of loans in such a way as to protect loans that might have

been made prior to the awarding of a licence which could have been cancelled under existing regulatory authority. If that is the intent of the amendment then, Mr. Speaker, with just one or two more comments we are quite prepared to let this bill go to committee for perusal. I trust the standing committee will give this bill fairly rapid consideration.
Any carrier must be subject to an over-all regulatory authority. Good laws should be applied to the interprovincial and international movement of goods and passengers. This is necessary for the sake of the industry as a whole and the proper and good order of the development of the movement of passengers and goods interprovincially and internationally. It must be subject to some over-all national regulatory authority, as well as being subject to agreements entered into by Canada with other nations with respect to the passage of goods and passengers from one country to another.
The minister has tended to over-complicate the situation a little bit. On the other hand the intent of the bill is clear. It is a good one and one we are prepared to let pass. As we read the bill and understand it, we hope there is a capacity for provincial governments to act singularly or in concert with adjacent provinces. I am referring to movement in a loan, debt or equity situation to assist a regional air carrier or a third level air carrier, a feeder air carrier, should they be faced with hard times. The uppermost question in my mind now is the question of the degree to which the federal government itself is an appropriate and proper vehicle, as opposed to provincial authorities, to move in the direction of assistance to Atlantic regional air carriers; to move into third level carrier service; and to strengthen and sustain its position as a regional air carrier in the country, with some stature and importance.
I hope the minister's statement embraced the principle of the right of the federal authority and the responsibility of the federal authority to move, before it becomes necessary for a collection of provincial authorities to move toward lending monetary support and assistance to a regional air carrier. I trust this bill does not interfere with that principle. At this point in time we do not see it, although it might be hidden, and we look forward to more in depth examination of it in committee. With those few comments, we are prepared to let the matter go through now.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 4, 1977, the minister issued a press release in connection with this bill from which I would like to quote as follows:
Transport Minister Otto Lang today introduced an amendment to the Aeronautics Act that would prohibit the purchase of an airline by a provincial government without federal permission.
This new amendment is in addition to Bill C-40, introduced last month, containing amendments to protect federal airports and airport sites from urban development encroaching on their boundaries.
The press release continues as follows:
Mr. Lang said the amendment, introduced today, "makes clear this government's intent to ensure that the purchase, scheduling and operation of air carriers in this country remain within federal jurisdiction."
May 25, 1977

Mr. Lang originally proposed such legislation following a decision by the Supreme Court of Canada to uphold the purchase of Pacific Western Airlines by the Alberta government.
The new amendment will prohibit the transfer of shares or the issuing of a licence to an international or interprovincial air carrier without approval of the federal government.
The amendment also gives the Canadian Transport Commission the authority to suspend or cancel the licence of any air carrier allowing the transfer of its shares or the acquisition of its debt by a province.
In introducing the bill today, the minister talked about difficulties regulatory agencies would have in dealing with an airline owned by a provincial government at arm's length, as it deals with the private carriers. We have a number of regulatory agencies that deal with issues which are of concern to provincial governments and on which provincial governments make representations. There is no hesitation on the part of these regulatory agencies to hear from provincial governments. Obviously they do not feel very threatened by hearing from them. Usually they do not listen to the provincial governments. This is a poor excuse for limiting the right of a provincial government to buy into or take over a privately owned airline if the provincial government believes it is in the interest of the people of its province to have such public ownership.
Had the minister had this power when the Conservative government of Alberta moved to take over Pacific Western Airlines, this minister and this federal government would have prevented the Alberta government from taking over PWA.
I would like to give two illustrations of government regulatory agencies which have heard from provincial governments on issues of importance to the people of those provinces. Those agencies have not felt intimidated, threatened or anything else by those representations. The CTC, until recently the CRTC, has to rule on applications for rate increases made by Bell Canada for telephones in Ontario or Quebec, and it has to rule on applications for rate increases in British Columbia made by B.C. Telephone. They have had representations made to them on behalf of the citizens of their provinces by some of the provincial governments, in which they have objected to the size of the rate increase asked for, or have objected to any rate increase. After the CTC has heard from those provincial governments, it has made decisions based on their independent findings. Similarly the CTC has repeatedly dealt with applications for freight rate increases by the railways, increases to which the provincial governments of Manitoba, Saskatchewan and Alberta have objected. There has been no difficulty on the part of CTC in studying the questions and making decisions. Usually it permits increases far greater than the provincial governments have agreed to, and yet it has not felt threatened.
It is a completely spurious argument on the part of the minister that the federal government needs to have the authority to stop provincial governments from doing things which they feel are in the best interests of their people. A provincial government which owns an airline or part of an airline would still require CTC approval for changes in rates and changes in routes. There is no reason why the CTC, the regulatory agency, could not deal with an application made by an airline
Aeronautics Act
owned by a provincial government in the same way as it deals with applications made by airlines owned by private industry.
We have had no explanation from the minister or any other minister of what policies are being followed. What are the principles upon which the government bases its desire to prohibit provincial governments from getting into the airline business?
I know the minister was amazed and shocked, as I am sure were Conservative members, by the action of the Alberta government in buying all the shares of Pacific Western Airlines. I can just imagine what would have happened if that purchase had been made by the former NDP government of British Columbia. The government of Alberta apparently decided it was in the interests of the people of Alberta to have control of the service which PWA was providing, that the province was not going to be bound, I presume, purely by whether or not a given route made profit or showed a loss. The province wanted to provide the best possible service it could to the people of Alberta. If the minister had any logical objections to that purchase by the Alberta government of Pacific Western Airlines, he has certainly never made them known in this House or, to my knowledge, explained them publicly.
There are a number of other regional airlines in addition to PWA. For example, Transair operated in Manitoba, Ontario and the Northwest Territories. It was a privately owned airline which got into difficulties, 1 suppose caused by the cost of fuel mainly, which has increased so substantially that the airline found it could no longer make a profit. From what we read in the newspapers, apparently a proposal was put forward that PWA, now owned by the Alberta government, should buy Transair. I do not think the Minister of Transport discussed the matter with the premier of the province of Manitoba, in whose province the overhaul base for Transair has been located for many years.
The Leader-Post for May 6, 1977, carries a news story which in part reads as follows:
The CBC says Pacific Western Airlines, owned by the Alberta government, is expected to announce shortly that it will acquire Transair Ltd.
A deal has been made, and I think only a few details remain to be ironed out before it is concluded. The news story continues:
The report says the acquisition of the Winnipeg based regional airline will have the blessing of the federal government.
I wonder why it has the blessing of the federal government when the federal government was opposed to the purchase by the Alberta government of Pacific Western Airlines.
The report says Pacific Western will take over Transair for about $5 millions. .. Transair has lost about $6.5 million in its last two fiscal years.
CBC says it is understood that the federal goverment approached PWA to consider takeover of PWA. The government tried to prevent the Alberta government from buying PWA in the first place.
The report continues:
One of the most important aspects of the acquisition is the routes PWA would pick up. It could serve the whole of western Canada from Winnipeg to Victoria.

The report says that as part of the deal, Transair will lose its Winnipeg to Toronto run, which will be assumed by Air Canada. But Transair will pick up additional routes in western Canada, giving the airline inter-city service between Winnipeg, Regina, Saskatoon, Calgary and Edmonton.
The report says Air Canada will give the takeover its blessing as will the government of Saskatchewan. Manitoba is expected to follow suit, as long as it is guaranteed that maintenance facilities will remain in Winnipeg.
I understand that the government of Saskatchewan is, to say the least, not enthused by this deal, and that the government of Manitoba is not happy with the deal either. In any case, I see no reason for giving this government, parlicularly this minister, this kind of power. The minister has moved to take power-which he does not need-to do things which he has never explained, to take power to do things regarding which he has never enunciated the basic principles, to take power which, in our view, he wants purely for political reasons. We certainly cannot agree to that.
As we understand it, Mr. Speaker, this bill amends several sections of the Aeronautics Act. Basically it is aimed at prohibiting the purchase of an extrapovincial-interprovincial or international-airline without federal permission.
The Aeronautics Act is divided into three parts. Part I deals with the duties of the minister and regulations that the minister may prescribe regarding safety and inspection. Part II of the act, sections 9 to 19, deals with the Canadian Transport Commission and its role in civil aviation. The main role of the Canadian Transport Commission is licensing air routes and supervisions of rates. Part III deals with the hiring of personnel to administer the act and Department of Transport documents. The relationship between the ministry and the CTC is basically that the CTC grants a licence to a carrier to operate an air service and supervises the rates, and the ministry takes steps to ensure that the aircraft is operated safely.
This bill, along with Bill C-40, prohibits the transfer of the shares of an extraprovincial air carrier to a province without the approval of the governor in council. The new subsection 16(2) would prohibit the issuance of a licence to an extraprovincial air carrier in which a province is in the process of acquiring a debt or equity interest without the approval of the governor in council, which means-without the approval of the minister. This subsection would apply only to applications for new licences; it does not affect existing licensing. In other words, the minister is not prepared to take on the government of Alberta for its purchase of Pacific Western Airlines.
This bill adds a new subsection 16(8.1) which directs the commission to suspend an existing licence of a provincial air carrier where the carrier allows a transfer of shares without the approval of the governor in council, or where the carrier allows a province to acquire a debt interest.
The complementary bill, Bill C-40, also has an amendment to section 16 of the Aeronautics Act, which is the section at which Bill C-46 is aimed. Bill C-40 provides an amendment to 16(3) and 16(8) which would enable the issuance of licences for non-scheduled air services upon proof of public interest, rather than proof of public convenience and necessity as now required.
(Mr. Orlikow.)
This provision may be detrimental, depending upon the definition given to "public interest". Under the old rule of public convenience and necessity, an applicant must prove that his service would add something. Under the public interest rule, if the public interest is to be defined as section 3 of the National Transportation Act, then the public interest is defined in terms of competition and the economic well-being of Canada. However, if the public interest is to be defined as section 3 of the amended National Transportation Act after Bill C-33 is passed, then the public interest is defined in terms of competition and commercial viability of the carriers.
Since the tabling of the Hall report we have heard the minister say several times how pleased he was with the main provisions of the report and that he was going to move to implement them. If the Hall report made one thing clear, it was that commercial viability is not a good way of judging what is needed in terms of transportation.
Let me quote from an article by Nicholas Hills which appeared in the Montreal Gazette on May 18 of this year, dealing with the Hall report. It reads:
Hall has gone almost all the way to meeting the arguments of the western premiers that the railways and Ottawa are the barriers to a new economic future, based on fairer tariff, tax and freight rate policies .. .
He has said, like the western premiers in every political strife, that the raw materials should be processed here, and not in central Canada.
He has inferred, again like the western premiers, that the railways engage in duplicity-for having settled the west originally they now want to settle its future, again to their advantage.
In another article on May 18, which I will not quote but the headline of which reads: "Hall Flies in Face of Lang Philosophy", Nick Hills makes precisely the point. The minister wants this authority because he does not want the provinces to go into the airline business because they may not be interested in just commercial viability and just in making profit. They may be interested in giving service to the people of their provinces. That, of course, is anathema to the Minister of Transport. He continues, despite all the nice things he says about the Hall report, with his basic philosophy that all that counts is making a profit. We oppose that.
We think that if a province wants to go into the airline business to provide a better service for its people, it should have that right, and it should not have to come cap in hand to the minister or to the government to ask for permission to do it. That does not mean that the other provisions in the Aeronautics Act and the other acts which apply to the present or future private operators of airlines will not continue, that the provinces will not have to meet the standards with regard to the safety of the service and everything else, but we see no reason why this government should prohibit any provincial government, regardless of political stripe, which wants to go into the business, from doing so. There is more than Pacific Western Airlines involved in this question.
There are a number of regional carriers. There is Eastern Airlines which provides service in the Atlantic provinces, there is Quebec Air which provides service in Quebec, and there are
May 25, 1977

some regional carriers in Ontario. Given the increased cost of fuel and of parts, it may be that one or the other of these regional carriers would decide that they can no longer make a profit, in spite of subsidies on profitable routes which the federal government is sometimes persuaded to provide. It may be that they may want to go out of business and that one of the provincial governments will say, "This service is so important to Nova Scotia, Newfoundland or northern Quebec that we will take over this airline and we will run it, not to make a profit but to provide service". What this bill would say is that they could not do it without satisfying the federal government of the day, the Department of Transport or the Minister of Transport, that they have a valid reason for doing it.
We see no reason why the federal government needs that authority; we see no reason for putting these restrictions on any provincial government, and we will oppose this bill.
