subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA

speakeroldname: Hon. Otto E. Lang (Minister of Transport) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Transport; Minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board
subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext:
that Bill C-17, respecting the reorganization of Air Canada, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.
He said: Mr. Speaker, it is 40 years since parliament gave authority, in the Trans-Canada Air Lines Act of 1937, for the establishment of our national airline. We may all, I think, take satisfaction and indeed pride in the work done by our predecessors in the House and by the directors and officers of the company itself in providing for and developing one of the world's great airlines.
In the early years of its development, Trans-Canada Air Lines mainly carried mails while it expanded its fleet, trained its staff, and provided advice on the airfields and aids to navigation which were required for the introduction of passenger services across the continent.
By 1939, TCA had expanded to the point where it employed 500 people and in that year carried 21,000 passengers on domestic services. Its fleet was comprised mainly of Lockheed 14H aircraft which could accommodate 11 passengers and 2,700 pounds of cargo, and could cruise at 200 miles per hour over typical stage lengths of 350 miles.
By way of contrast, after four decades of operation in peace and war, Air Canada by the end of 1975 had over 20,000 employees. In that year it carried 10.4 million revenue passen-
Air Canada
gers, roughly one quarter of whom travelled on international routes. The corporation's fleet consisted of 120 aircraft, ranging from 365-seat Boeing 747s to 95 seat DC-9s.
The employment of jet aircraft, starting in the early 1960's, permitted very rapid rates of growth in the airline's productivity. Cruising speeds rose to the region of 550 miles per hour over stage lengths of up to 4,000 miles.
This increase in the speed of air transportation, combined with the increases in productivity which allowed airlines to hold back on price increases and even to make price reductions while paying increasingly higher wages and salaries to their employees, brought about dramatic changes in travelling patterns. Travel for pleasure or personal reasons has gradually replaced business travel as the main source of business in many markets. This in turn has led airlines to become involved in many new types of associated activities such as hotels, vacation package tours, and computerized teleprocessing systems.
Despite this rapid pace of change in the air transport industry, the original Trans-Canada Air Lines Act was changed only slightly over the years, the key amendments being in 1945 and 1953, and in 1964, when the name of the corporation was changed to Air Canada. The change of name was symbolic of the wider horizons in which the airline had come to operate, not only in the national but increasingly in an international sphere.
The act incorporating the company, enacted when a transcontinental flight was itself a major undertaking, has become less and less appropriate to the evolving needs of the day. Therefore we have thoroughly revised the old Air Canada Act to enable the corporation to respond quickly and effectively to the challenges of the future.
Underlying Bill C-17 is the fact that Air Canada is no longer a fledgling airline and no longer needs the special protective measures which are incorporated in the present act and in the Aeronautics Act. The corporation, nevertheless, faces new challenges and must be able to adjust to changing conditions. The bill seeks to put Air Canada on a footing similar to that of the airlines with which it competes.
First, there is the matter of ownership. In 1937 it seemed appropriate that organizations with experience in transportation should be asked to organize a trans-Canada airline, and after exploration of various possibilities the Canadian National Railway became the sole shareholder. It provided not only the share capital but also the first president of the airline and the administrative services required to support him in running the operation. As it has grown over the year, Air Canada has become less and less dependent upon the direct support of the Canadian National Railway. Therefore the bill provides for the cancellation of the shares now held by the CNR. All Air Canada shares will be held directly by the government.
Associated with this change, the present arrangement whereby the auditors of CN are by legislation also the auditors for Air Canada should be discontinued. Therefore, the bill

May 25, 1977
Air Canada
provides for the appointment of Air Canada's auditors by the governor in council, and generally brings the provisions associated with an outside audit into line with other recently created Crown corporations.
The bill contains no reference to the Air Canada contract nor to the airmail contract except inferentially. The 1937 act described the trans-Canada contract in some detail, provided for a conterminous mail contract, and stipulated how the airmail rates in each year should be adjusted according to whether the corporation recorded a surplus or a deficit during the preceding year. That latter practice was discontinued following the revision of the act in 1945.
In 1953 the section describing Trans-Canada Airlines' contract was shortened. To be specific, references to a schedule of services to be maintained by the corporation under the contract and to the payment of a subsidy equal to any deficit at the end of the year were deleted. The present Air Canada Act also contains clauses dealing with what is now called the Air Canada contract and the Air Canada mail contract. Provisions for payment of subsidies are included in the act only with regard to contracts containing terms ordered by the governor in council into which the minister may enter with subsidiaries of Air Canada.
It is my view that there is a better way to arrange these particular relationships between the government and Air Canada. Accordingly, the Air Canada contract and the airmail contract would be cancelled, and no provision for the payment of subsidies to Air Canada directly, or to any of its subsidiaries, is contained in the bill. Instead, Air Canada would be required to comply with directions from the governor in council. We will in the later stages, following discussions we have had within the government, introduce an amendment which will qualify the text as it now appears so that the directions which may be given by the governor in council will be directions of a general nature.
This is designed, as I will mention later, to emphasize the fact that it is not the intention nor the purpose of the government to give directions in relation to the day-to-day operations of the airline. It is our view that the airline ought to make those judgments on its operations as a part of its own management decisions and that we ought not to interfere with that.
In the bill we are providing compensation to the corporation if compliance with the directions given to it results in losses to Air Canada. This is in line with the 1975 transportation policy statement that where the government requires certain services to be performed at a certain cost, that cost ought to be known, and it ought generally to be borne by the treasury rather than be passed on to the users of the transportation service.
The discontinuance of the Air Canada contract has another consequence which should receive our collective attention. Under the Aeronautics Act the CTC is now compelled to issue licences to Air Canada for services provided pursuant to the Air Canada contract.
It is now proposed that Air Canada should apply to the CTC for new licences in the same way as other carriers do.

This change is in line with the emphasis that the government and, indeed, the board and senior management of the corporation place on the need for Air Canada to compete on a similar footing with other airlines.
I remarked earlier that changed circumstances have -created new needs as well as removed the necessity for old safeguards. The present act contains a list of the business and powers of the corporation which, although long, is not sufficiently comprehensive in terms of the new activities which have now become associated with air transport. Whereas the provisions of the present act are quite specific and narrow, we have taken a much broader approach. This bill provides more flexibility for businesses and activities in areas associated with the operations of major airlines while retaining control by the government over Air Canada as a Crown corporation against entry into areas not related to the airline business. There always remains a risk in any enumeration of powers, no matter how broadly drafted, that some future legitimate activity is not provided for in it. To ensure that Air Canada does not become the prisoner of that kind of situation, the governor in council would be given power to authorize the corporation to engage in activities which are not specifically provided for in the bill.
Under the present act Air Canada's authorized equity capital has an upper limit of $25 million. The actual issued capital is $5 million, whereas the corporation's current balance sheet lists total assets in excess of $1 billion. The present arrangement forces Air Canada to obtain most of the financing it requires in the form of long-term debt. This, in turn, has three undesirable effects. First, it makes it difficult to compare Air Canada's performance with that of major airlines which have debt equity ratios over a wide range, but none so extreme and debt-laden as 97 to 3, which is currently the case with Air Canada.
Second, since nearly all of Air Canada's financing is in the form of debt which carries a charge against current operations in the form of interest payments, Air Canada can swing very quickly between a profit and a loss on the basis of very slight changes in the market or in operating conditions.
Third, lenders in the long-term debt market apply certain tests before supplying funds, and one of these tests involves a satisfactory debt equity ratio.
Under present circumstances Air Canada stands little chance of being able to borrow in the market without government guarantees. Since the intention of Bill C-17 is to pave the way for a more commercially oriented corporation, Air Canada must have a more normal debt equity ratio to pass the test applied in the money market.
Therefore Bill C-17 makes the following provisions: The authorized capital of the corporation would be $750 million. There may be available to Air Canada up to $750 million in direct government loans or government guaranteed loans obtained in the open market. In addition, over and above the $1.5 billion just mentioned, the corporation would have the power to borrow money in the market on its own credit. For long-term debt-that is to say, debt which exceeds 18 months in term-prior approval from the Minister of Finance would
May 25, 1977

be required, but short-term borrowing, to accommodate cyclical short-term cash needs, would not require that approval. The existing debt can be rearranged by converting some of the existing government debt to equity, some of the existing CNR debt to equity, or a combination of these, but the bill puts a limit on these conversions of $600 million. If the corporation's debt to CNR were converted to equity capital, CNR's own debt to the government would be correspondingly reduced in an offset against the reduction which was made in that manner.
These provisions do not establish a specific debt-equity ratio that would be maintained indefinitely. Instead, they provide a framework within which a healthy debt-equity ratio can be maintained by the performance of the airline or by provision of new capital on the analogy of private companies seeking new equity or debt. The mechanisms for infusions of up to $750 million each for equity capital and government debt were based on that premise. The statutory appropriations are balanced by the dollar ceilings which may not be exceeded.
To arrive at the $750 million figure, estimates were made of Air Canada's probable capital requirements over the next five years and these data were combined with existing long-term debt and equity and a safety factor was then applied.
I would like to add that Air Canada would be allowed to borrow on its own credit without limit. If Air Canada is successful commercially, and I believe it will be, the corporation should be in a position to borrow on the open market within a very short period of time.
Here I wish to add a note of emphasis. It is the intention both of myself and of the board and senior management of Air Canada that its performance will be equal to or better than the performances of the world's top airlines. That means that it must be competitive in every way. It is possible, for example, for an airline virtually to assure on-time departures of all its flights if it is prepared to pay the cost of over-capacity in its fleet. Equally it is possible for an airline to return profits by combining under-capacity with a monopoly. It will be the responsibility of the board of Air Canada, to me as minister, to parliament and to the people of Canada, to achieve the maximum possible efficiency in all aspects of the airline's operation, and not to favour one aspect at the expense of the others. One measure of their success will be the financial results of the company, and it is the intention of the government that Air Canada will conduct its operations in contemplation of profit.
I have of course referred earlier to the power reserved to the governor in council to give directives to the corporation, and for compensation, subject to appropriation by parliament, to be paid for losses incurred in giving effect to such directives. This gives the government power to ensure that any tendency to concentrate on profit at the expense of necessary but loss-creating services can be countered. But it will also ensure that such services are clearly identified and the social benefits achieved will be at the cost of the treasury and not of Air Canada.
Air Canada
As I said earlier that is consistent with the principle we have been applying in other areas to railways as well as to Air Canada. We ought to know specifically what it costs if a particular social obligation or other obligation is imposed upon an entity like this and we ought to identify and pay that cost so that the airline or railway in question is not left in the position of either being short of cash to perform its necessary functions or of having to charge more for other services it provides in order to make up the loss on the services to be performed.
The inquiry conducted by the Hon. W. Z. Estey in 1975 resulted in a number of recommendations for changes in the present Air Canada Act. Some of these recommendations have been taken into account, as I have indicated previously, and are in the bill. The bill also addresses the matter of capacities and activities of the corporation and provides for direct government ownership and government directives to which I referred.
In addition, the bill reflects a careful consideration of recommendations contained in the Estey report, such as the expansion of the board of directors to 15 members and their appointment by the governor in council. Here I may say that it will not be our intention to move to fill all these positions immediately but to do so progressively over a period of time. Further recommendations of the Estey report were that the chairman and president be appointed by the government after consultations with the board; bylaws passed by the board to be subject to government approval; and power to the board to delegate duties to an executive committee which must be established.
In addition, the bill contains an innovation which would allow Air Canada to create subsidiaries, subject to the approval of the governor in council. Under the present act, it is the governor in council who, upon petition by Air Canada, can create companies whose shares are subsequently acquired by Air Canada.
Finally I should say a few words about the legal framework of the bill.
Basically, Air Canada would continue as in the past to be a "special act" corporation, but certain provisions of the Canada Business Corporations Act would be incorporated in the special act.
For example, the bill has adopted the "natural person" concept which says that Air Canada can do all things that a "natural person" can do, but with the qualification that this "natural person" power is confined to activities listed in the bill.
Due to the fact that Air Canada's permitted activities are set out, and that its "natural person" power is restricted to these permitted activities, the doctrine of ultra vires would continue to apply to Air Canada. In order to protect third parties from finding themselves in a position in which Air Canada has acted beyond its capacities, thus rendering a transaction null and void, the bill expressly provides that such ultra vires acts by the corporation may not be used against third parties which have acted in good faith.

May 25, 1977
Air Canada
The bill also contains a number of "housekeeping" clauses. Generally speaking, they describe the relationship between this bill and other statutes.
I have had discussions with Air Canada and others since first reading of the bill and I shall, in the standing committee, propose certain amendments to the bill. Some are intended to ease and facilitate the workings of the corporation, some are intended to be clarification if there is any possibility of doubt about the meaning of a clause, but in its essence the bill remains the same as it is now at second reading.
In committee some substantial amendments will attempt to give the assurance of greater commercial flexibility to Air Canada in order not to impede it in its operations and its competitiveness with other airlines. Changes will be suggested to bring some greater correspondence between the special act and the terms of the Canada Business Corporations Act. In some cases it is a matter of removing doubt about the meaning of a clause in the special act as drafted.
More important, as I indicated earlier there will be the intention to narrow the directive power which is set out in the bill so that it is limited to directions of a general nature. Again I emphasize that is designed to underline the fact that Air Canada should be run essentially by its management and its board of directors who are accountable to the shareholders and to the minister for the people of Canada in the same way as the management of other corporations is, but not subjected to day-to-day interference in those operations. It is not the intention of the government to get into the day-to-day management but rather to leave that to the best management possible for Air Canada.
We also propose to clarify the legal status of Air Canada. While not really believing there is much doubt about it as the special act is written, to resolve any possible doubt we will be prepared to have an amendment put before the committee which will make it clear that Air Canada is not in law or in fact an agent of Her Majesty. That will perhaps serve to further emphasize the nature of the airline as we see it and our objective that it continue to be a first-class world level airline; that it be competitive; that it apply good business principles and that it serve the people of Canada by operating effectively and efficiently and, one hopes, with constantly improved attitudes by all who serve and work in it.
I should like to add some comments on that very point, Mr. Speaker. Air Canada, like any other company, will so often provide good service or better service depending on the total attitude of those who work in it. I pay tribute to the men and women who work in the company, to top management and to all other levels, and express the hope that with the new attitude being shown to Air Canada and its future, and the new approach of its present management, to whom I pay special tribute, there will be constant improvement in the morale and attitude of those who work within the corporation.
While one hopes, as a member of the government or of the travelling public, for efficient service from any air transport
[Mr. Lang.)
company, one may be permitted to have special reasons for wanting it in the case of Air Canada, the shareholders of which are all the people of Canada. I look forward to full discussion on the details of this bill in committee and commend this bill to hon. members and its reference to the Standing Committee on Transport and Communications.

subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, if I had known this bill was to be discussed so soon, I suggest I would be in a position to make more co-ordinated and lucid comments on it.
More than 12 years ago members spoke in this Chamber on the necessity of separating Air Canada from Canadian National Railways. This bill does that and it is an historic, significant occasion in this the 40th year of Air Canada operations. The airline has finally come of age. It has groaned and moaned for 40 years. In the next 40 years I hope Air Canada will get up off its knees, walk, run, and ultimately fly. Let it provide a service of which Canadians will be proud, and which will bring us prestige as international operators of air carrier service. Of course when I speak of Air Canada service I speak of the total package of services which must be associated with air service.
The bill gives Air Canada the right to enter into activities not directly related to flying, activities such as catering to the tourist trade. I hope we can not only be proud of Air Canada service, but that its service will grow constantly better. The people of Canada still own the airline, and I prophesy they will own it in years to come.
The airline's debt ratio at 97 to three is poor. We are about to reduce that ratio; that is a good and necessary step. If the airline is to enter the market place for financing, its debt ratio should be in the order of 60 to 40, or 50-50. I suspect, from the way the airline has operated in the last ten or 15 years, that the government will come to this House from time to time to suggest methods for injecting more equity capital into Air Canada, in order to sustain its debt-equity ratio. That ratio must be adequate if the airline is to enter the market place to secure the finances for its operating needs. I hope it will not happen, and I do not intend to begin my remarks in a negative manner.
This House and the standing committee will need to consider in depth some of the proposals contained in the bill. Perhaps I might mention some of the ways Air Canada is to be reorganized under Bill C-17. Basically, the bill would separate Air Canada from its parent, Canadian National. It contains four fundamental proposals. First, it would authorize Air Canada to engage in a wider range of activities. Second, it would separate Air Canada from the CNR; the airline would be an entity unto itself. I remind the House that, to the best of my knowledge, it has been the policy of my party for at least 15 years to separate Air Canada from the CNR. We first heard this might happen when the present Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Jamieson) was minister of transport. We heard nothing after that one-line comment made years ago in a budget debate.
May 25, 1977

Third, the bill would authorize Air Canada to increase its capital stock. This we consider to be necessary. Fourth, it would authorize Air Canada to seek debt financing in the market place. All these points relate to the question of management, on which the minister touched, and to the necessity of improving Air Canada's debt-equity ratio in order that it may go to the market place for its operation funds. Each of those points is worth exploring in detail.
First, let us consider the question of broader powers. Air Canada is rather restricted by the terms of the present act in the type of activities in which it can engage. The proposed act broadens the capacities and activities which the company may undertake, both within and outside Canada. Aside from operating the business of an air carrier, there are references to hotels and other accommodation, surface vehicles and facilities for the transportation and housing of persons, goods and mail; services, facilities and equipment for organizing and conducting tours, catering and providing other passenger-related services, including reservations for transportation and accommodation; and computer and tele-processing systems and technical, advisory and consulting services.
Perhaps in committee we shall discover how far those powers extend. Hon. members no doubt are aware of the events which preceded Judge Estey's examination of Air Canada activities, and know how close Air Canada came to breaking this country's law, and know how some officials in the not too distant past stopped Air Canada breaking the law.
As well, the new act permits the company to establish or invest in subsidiary companies, provided authorization of the governor in council, which means the federal cabinet or the minister, is first obtained. These changes will enable the company to offer a greater range 6f services and to engage in other activities which may be deemed finanially beneficial. This provision would put right that which Air Canada officials were doing which was wrong. I do not mind doing that. I am confident that most members of this House believe as I do. If Air Canada is to operate successfully, it must operate in areas broader than the simple carriage of passengers and goods. It must engage in other activities. There is general agreement on this side of the Chamber with regard to that.
We will want to look very closely at Judge Estey's suggestions with regard to this expanded authority. That will be done here in the Chamber and in greater detail in committee.
With regard to ownership of the capital stock transfer envisaged by this bill, up until this time all of this stock has been held by CNR, a Crown corporation. What is envisaged here is the establishment of a Crown corporation, albeit subject to the business act, business practices act and so on. Nevertheless, we are establishing another Crown corporation.
This House could well spend a day of its time in the not too distant future looking at the role of Crown corporations and the use to which the government puts the concept of Crown corporations with regard to transportation in Canada. There is VIA rail, if it ever gets any money and gets off the ground.
Air Canada
CN is in an unhealthy position as a result of Air Canada. I do not mind it being a bit of a whipping boy. These things are relatively important as CN, the principal shareholder of Air Canada, has been saddled with enormous debt ever since the birth of Air Canada.
We established VIA as a Crown corporation. We are looking at Canadian National Marine Transportation as a Crown corporation. Now we are looking at Air Canada as a separate Crown corporation with what might be considered as extraordinary authority and power.
The minister undertook this afternoon to deal with the authority implicit in this bill, in the VIA arrangements, in the arrangements for Canadian National Marine Corporation and, indeed, extended to communications.
In the new Communications Act there is implicit clear authority for daily intervention on the part of the minister to ensure that policy and policy guidelines are being followed, not by the boards of directors of these corporations, but by the day-to-day executive of these corporations.
We on this side of the Chamber have argued for many years that there has to be greater political control in the sense of ensuring that the will of Canadians with respect to these tools of all Canadians is the will of the government and parliament, and is being followed. Never did we suggest that that authority go so far as to permit the minister to intervene on a day-to-day basis with the nuts and bolts operation of any of these Crown corporations engaged in transportation matters. That is one matter that will be looked at very closely.
I come back to the ownership and position of Air Canada, that position being one of a wholly owned subsidiary of Canadian National. CN, exercising its proper right and authority, appointed five shareholders to the Air Canada board of directors while the governor in council appointed four.
The proposed act stipulates that shares of Air Canada shall be held by the Minister of Transport in trust for Her Majesty in right of Canada and that the shares are not transferable. It further provides that the corporation shall be under the management of a board of directors comprised of a chairman and president and not more than 13 other directors. What a pork barrel that will be. All of them will be appointed by the governor in council.
As long as the Minister of Transport holds in right of the Crown all of the shares of Air Canada and maintains the right to appoint the chairman and board of directors by order in council, anything to the contrary will be opposed by us if there is an exercise capable of demonstrating an authority to intervene at other than the directors level.
If the minister and the government want statutory authority to intervene and interfere, it is and will remain our position, until we see and are satisfied with the amendments promised a few moments ago by the minister to clarify this, that that is where there shall be ministerial intervention with respect to "policy guidelines". That is where the minister should do it, not at the day to day working level of Air Canada. These are areas we have to look at closely.

May 25, 1977
Air Canada
We have to look at the authorized share capital. There is a concern in the industry. Indeed Air Canada is concerned with regard to the minimum authorized share capital presently held by it. I think it amounts to S25 million. This amount, together with the accumulated net profits of the corporation, labelled retained earnings, an interesting chartered accountant's view of a damnably high debt the taxpayer has to pay, represents the shareholder's equity. On December 31, 1975, the balance sheet totalled $31.4 million.
I repeat to the minister that we had hoped that the standing committee would have an opportunity to examine the annual report of Air Canada before dealing with Bill C-17. The failure of the government to refer the annual report of Air Canada in each of the last three years is reprehensible. Indeed it could be argued that CN by its association acted illegally for several years. It was not until quite recently that we bothered to obey the law by approving certain of the annual acts that came before us with respect to this.
The same balance sheet shows that the company had long term debt of $1,011.4 million. That is already out of date. There is no question about it. These figures are mentioned because it is in this way that you get the relationship between the $1,011.4 million and the $31.4 million shareholders' equity, comprised of some loans and retained earnings. This puts Air Canada in the desperate situation of a debt ratio of 97 to 3. This means that 97 per cent had to come from borrowing while only 3 per cent represents the shareholders' original investment, plus accumulated net profits.
Someone like myself from the Atlantic provinces who watches this government cannot forget that we have massive debt in rail passenger service in the Atlantic provinces. My God, a desperate debt! If we ran rail passenger trains at the current rate of debt we would never get anywhere with this kind of debt. Yet they are going to write this off. They are going to take our trains away from us; we are going to get buses. We are going to ride from Saint John to Montreal on a bus so we can catch the transcontinental train. I wonder what Joe Howe would say about that if he were here today.
Bill C-17 authorizes Air Canada to issue common shares up to the amount of $750 million, if I read it correctly. It provides for the conversion of part of the existing debt to common shares which, of course, can only be sold to the government. If I understood the minister correcty, $750 million, in that sense, is the upper limit. This may not necessarily be issued with the passage of the bill before us, but in combination with the use of other methods of accepting other debt instruments of Air Canada it will at some point in time virtually absorb the debt of $1 billion or more that is there. I hope I understand this correctly because it is important that I should tell the minister that this is the position in which we are in general agreement. Indeed we cannot see any other way of approaching this problem caused by the existing and mounting debt of Air Canada.

Over the years Air Canada's need for capital has virtually been met in entirety by borrowing from the government. The proposed act would provide Air Canada with a much greater flexibility in raising funds. We welcome this. In addition to the substantial increase in common shares which can be issued to the government, the company is permitted to borrow from the government. But most important is the freedom to borrow from the long term capital account provided approval has been obtained from the minister of finance. I assume this approval has to be transmitted to Air Canada through the Ministry of Transport. We suggest that this is a form of monitoring which should continue to take place. I suppose that is the only truly logical way for this to happen. We assume it will take place by way of a single resolution before the House which would either be approved or rejected-in the latter case the department would have to find some other way in which to operate.
There is no limit to the amount of borrowing into which Air Canada can enter. We have some concern about the method to be employed by the government, and particularly by the minister, in exercising control over this very broad authority. This is the second area of major concern to those of us on this side. Again, we shall be dealing with it in some depth as the debate continues. Unless the minister is optimistic enough to think that this bill is going through this afternoon, or tomorrow, or Friday, or Monday, I caution him that there are a lot of my hon. friends over here who are concerned to deal with this measure in some depth.
Air Canada is this year celebrating its fortieth anniversary. Yet since 1937 there have been no fundamental amendments to the Air Canada Act. The minister has dealt with Judge Estey's report and has given us some indication of his intention to move with respect to certain of his recommendations which are referred to in the bill itself. Also, he has indicated that there are others which are not dealt with in the bill, and we shall be seeking clarification of the position taken by the minister toward them.
A number of the recommendations in the Estey Report continue to cause us considerable concern, especially those relating to Air Canada's management structure. For example there is the recommendation which states that the position of the board of directors as the ultimate authority should be improved by enlarging the board and forming an executive committee of the board. It is further stated that the independence and stature of the members of the board should be assured by giving statutory tenure and ensuring standards of appointments. In this connection it occurs to us-and I am referring to the last sentence-that it is incumbent upon us to make sure that attention is directed to this area and that an amendment is made accordingly. I say this because it seems to me that standards of qualifications of directors are just as important, when it comes to directors, as the maintenance of the government's right to appoint, arising from the fact that it is the principal shareholder.
Apart from statutory tenure and standards of appointment, we want qualification for appointments to be spelt out clearly. This is not the case at the present time. We want to know, and
May 25, 1977

I believe the travelling public and those engaged in the transportation industry want to know what the standards of qualifications for appointments are. They should be spelt out very clearly, in the bill. Further in his report, Judge Estey stated:
The independence of the board in its role as the ultimate interna] element of corporate control should be implanted securely and obviously in the statute.
I come back to what I was saying earlier about implicit authority in Bill C-17 and other bills which have been and which will be before us, giving power to the minister and to other ministers to intervene directly in the day to day operations of Crown corporations. This is somewhat repugnant to us on this side. On the other hand, we shall support and encourage his position with respect to his ministerial right to intervene at the board level. The minister has already indicated he is prepared to go further in this regard by way of certain clarifications.
I quote again from Estey. Indeed, Glassco in earlier reports touched on this aspect.
Finally, the method of appointing directors should be examined. The operation of the Corporation has now attained such proportions as to be a top-ranking national asset. Thus the board performs a fiduciary role of such importance that consideration should be given to its enlargement and to some prescribed standards of qualification or experience, prohibited interests, tenure, etc. etc. to ensure in the future a high level of board competence and independence. There seems no longer to be the original need to have a majority of the directors of Air Canada chosen from the membership of the CNR Board. Certainly the office of the president should be placed on an articulated basis or abolished. If retained he should be a member of the board.
Estey in no way meant to insult the board of directors. Those who have read that particular statement, I am sure, have also read his clarification. The point he is making, with respect to clarification and qualification of the role of the chairman of the board, is that the qualifications for appointment, reappointment and tenure should be clearly known, articulated, and spelled out so that all Canadians would have the trust and faith they richly deserve in this new corporation in order for it to operate in the manner the minister has described. Without it we could have some doubts as to whether it would survive.
Judge Estey's recommendations in this respect are fairly important. I would like to cite the following, which will be the last one, although I would like to go on for another hour or two:
The Air Canada Act should provide a channel for the government or the responsible minister to issue to the board of directors of the corporation policy directives where the national interest from time to time requires.
That indicates to me Judge Estey was saying there is an institutional responsibility, a parliamentary responsibility, a ministerial responsibility, and a government responsibility. If we interpret this recommendation and its translation into the act correctly, then I think we understand something which will be welcomed by all members in this Chamber. I am referring to the vehicle to pose questions to the minister, which he may not answer simply by saying, "I will bring your representation to the attention of the appropriate Air Canada board or
Air Canada
authority". That was never enough for this institution and will never be enough for this institution in the foreseeable future.
We require the right to examine the minister with respect to the degree to which he maintains a capacity to ensure that the board of directors is on top of his guidelines and policies and that they are in fact being implemented by the day to day corporate and executive management. It is through the board the minister must get his assurance, and it is through the board, with the ultimate passage of this particular bill, this Chamber will have the right to seek information, to make inquiries, to understand and to question without the minister being able to say "I cannot do anything with respect to it because it is out of my hands and I cannot touch it". When the minister becomes the holder of those shares and has the authority and governor in council approval to appoint directors, then let him tell me why it is we eat fried chicken every Friday from here to Halifax-cold, stale, sometimes fried chicken. Then let him stand up and tell me why we do not have the seats we richly deserve in the Atlantic provinces. Do not let him tell me then that he cannot tell me because he has no right to interfere. This is the type of interference we welcome and want. He knows the outlet of expression and the difficulties which arise when a minister does not feel obliged to respond to questions with respect to the carrier.
I am sorry this bill came up for debate today. I think the minister is going to get a little light-headed and start feeling big because various things are happening in his favour today. He gave $125 million to the Atlantic provinces. I publicly thank him for that. The sum of $100 million will go a way on highways for us. Perhaps Ponderosa Drive will be paved so that I can drive home over a paved road rather than a muddy one. We also welcome the $25 million which is ear-marked for bus and air support. I hope that $25 million will largely go into air, because this is an area where Air Canada has not been good to regional air carriers. I am not only referring to EPA, but other air carriers with respect to scheduling, paralleling of service, and the related problems this has caused particularly in the last 12 to 18 months.
We hope the minister's bill will get the fullest possible scrutiny. We hope he will respond frankly to us on the question of joint auditorship. We hope he will find the vehicle to name the Auditor General as a joint auditor, not only for this bill but for other Crown corporations dealing with transportation. The result of this would be that members of parliament would have a legitimate vehicle by which to examine the activities of Crown corporations such as Air Canada, Via Rail, Canadian National, Marine Transport and so on.
I will conclude by reminding the minister that the role of Crown corporations in transport relates to the realities of the day and the realities of the need to move our people comfortably and as economically as possible, and to move our goods and freight from one part of the country to another. It must operate in areas where the private sector cannot function as a tool of the economic stability of a region or as a tool of the economic development and growth of a region by way of having to maintain, because of federal regulatory authorities,

May 25, 1977
Air Canada
routes which are unprofitable. Unprofitable routings must be the responsibility of the people of Canada.
There is a will, not only in this Chamber but among the taxpayers of Canada, to ensure that best possible transportation modes are maintained and developed as need demonstrates. Where it is unprofitable and where there is a clear need for an economic stabilizing capacity or an economic development capacity, it can only be done by Crown corporations in my judgment. To that end I wish the minister well with his bill. There are three years of history waiting to be touched upon. I suggest the minister dust off his pants, sit down and listen. We will be here in July or August discussing this piece of legislation. I think it is worth it. When we are finished, I hope the minister has a good piece of legislation, and I hope Air Canada has a piece of legislation by which it can achieve the desired ends the minister mentioned in his concluding remarks.
To that end, the members of the opposition will lend the support they can. We hold out no promises of swift passage but rather, to the degree to which the minister is prepared to amend the shortcomings in the bill, to bring forward amendments that will overcome our difficulties with respect to it-to the degree he is able to do that and is prepared to do that, we will be prepared to support him in the passage of this legislation, and I look forward to speaking on it again at a later date.

subtopic: AIR CANADA ACT, 1976 MEASURE RESPECTING REORGANIZATION OF AIR CANADA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, members of the New Democratic Party, and CCF members who preceded the NDP, always supported Air Canada and always supported the concept of a publicly owned and operated transcontinental air carrier.
If all that this bill did, Mr. Speaker, was to split Air Canada off from the CNR and permit it to operate independently and more efficiently, we would have no objection to the bill. The bill itself is rather simple, providing for the setting up of Air Canada as a separate Crown corporation split away from CNR, which presently owns all the outstanding shares, and for some rearrangement of financial matters made necessary by this split. In addition, clause 8 makes the corporation directly liable to "comply with directions given to it in writing by the governor in council".
The other important change in this legislation is the modification of the system under the old Air Canada Act whereby the government contracted with Air Canada for the provision of services such as access to remote areas, passenger and freight services on sparsely populated runs, and so on. Clause 9 of the bill authorizes the government to modify this payment arrangement with Air Canada so that the former contract arrangement is replaced by government order, accompanied by a subsidy to cover the amount of loss incurred in carrying out the order.
We are opposed to this bill not because of what is in the bill or because of anything the minister said in his introduction today; we oppose it because of certain sections of the throne speech of last October and statements made by the minister
outside the House regarding what he sees as the future of Air Canada. Let me quote one passage in the throne speech:
In a further effort to reduce the size of government as well as expand the range of opportunities for private enterprise, all federal programs will be reviewed to identify those government activities which could be transferred to the private sector without reducing the quality of service to the public.
In January of this year the minister sent a letter to the chairman of the CNR indicating his intention to see this policy implemented. To this end he said he would like to see the CNR broken up into identifiable profit centres which could be auctioned off as units to the private sector. This very cogent critique of the situation was referred to in a column by Geoffrey Stevens which appeared in the Globe and Mail for January 20, 1977, and I should like to quote a few parts of his article. Mr. Stevens wrote this:
In the first eight years after the National Transportation Act came into force (in 1967), these subsidies totalled $646 million (compared to $334 million for the rival CPR).
He goes on to say that the CNR seems to have turned the corner so far as operating expenses are concerned and is in a position where it will shortly be making a small profit. He then asks a very simple question, one I think the minister should answer on some occasion, perhaps in closing this debate. Mr. Stevens asks:
If CN is going to start making money, why should private investors and stock market speculators reap the benefit? Why shouldn't the general public get something back for carrying the freight all these years? There's no law that says the taxpayer may only own enterprises that lose money.
I think Mr. Geoffrey Stevens makes a very pertinent comment. The splitting off of Air Canada from the CNR is the first evidence of this splitting off of these profit centres. The minister has admitted in interviews with the press that its purpose is the eventual privatization of Air Canada. To this end, the replacement of the old contract for a services relationship between the airline and the government has been replaced by a system of direct subsidization of unprofitable services, with the intention of putting Air Canada in the position of showing an accounting profit in order to make it more attractive to the private sector as a purchase.
The Minister of Transport has suggested that this relationship is the first step to the opening up of all of the former contracts for services routes to competitive bidding between Air Canada, CP and other airlines, which would have the effect of putting Air Canada on a completely commercial basis identical to that of CP, and increase the possibility of its being sold off as a unit to the private sector.
According to a CBC report on October 29, the minister said that he saw Air Canada eventually becoming a private corporation. He said that routes that now have to be operated by Air Canada whether it makes a profit or not, will not have to be operated by Air Canada whether it makes a profit or not, but will be open to competitive bidding and that the successful applicant will get the routes and the subsidy that goes with them. The minister said the reason behind the move was that he wanted Air Canada to be as profitable as possible so that it will be in a position where private ownership of the airline might be possible.

May 25, 1977

Simply put, what the minister wants is the money making routes identified and separated so that private investors would be willing to take over Air Canada-that is, the profitable part. This would mean that ultimately we would have a private airline operating the profitable sectors, such as transcontinental routes of which 75 per cent are now operated by Air Canada, and private carriers would operate losing routes with government subsidies. I come back to the question Geoffrey Stevens asked: where is it written that governments can only operate losing routes and should leave to the private investor, those who can afford to put money into making money, the profitable routes?
In an article on October 16 the Financial Post gave some indication of how the new legislation could affect this changeover. While the article was written before the first reading of the bill, it appears to have predicted the legislation as it is. According to the Financial Post of that date, a relatively small section of the bill sets out new operating rules for the airlines. Any additional operating instruction, such as new activities in air routes, would have to be spelled out by the Minister of Transport.
We have tried to check Bill C-17, Mr. Speaker, and it seems to us that what the Financial Post was referring to was the powers granted under clauses 8 and 9 of the bill. Clause 8 provides that Air Canada shall comply with directions given to it in writing by the governor in council. Clause 9 provides:
(1) The Governor in Council may
(a)	direct the method of calculation of any losses incurred by the corporation as a result of compliance with section 8;
(b)	direct that an audit be made of losses calculated pursuant to paragraph (a), and
(c)	determine the manner of payment of compensation to the corporation for losses verified pursuant to paragraph (b).
It seems to us that by this method money losing services will be identified and compensated for, and this would then fulfil the minister's objective of making Air Canada attractive to private investors. If that is true, Mr. Speaker, then we certainly cannot support the bill.
The minister keeps on talking about commercial viability and profitability. In the debate we had earlier on another bill I referred to how contrary that is to the basic principles enunciated by Mr. Justice Hall in the report which was tabled some days ago and with which the minister supposedly agrees.
The whole idea of commercial viability and profitability was attacked by the former minister of transport, Mr. Marchand. In June of 1975 he made a statement, and I should like to quote a few sentences from that statement to show how much the then minister was in opposition, at least according to the statement he made, to this whole concept, which this minister has enunciated since taking over this portfolio. Let me quote from that statement by the then minister of transport, Mr. Marchand, who said:
If you look at the size of this country and the distribution of its population you will see that you cannot have a transportation network which is economic everywhere; you cannot have an economic system of transportation to service the
Air Canada
north, for example, or to service those regions of the country where the population is very thin. You cannot have an economic system for regions which are remote from the centre.
Then he went on to say as follows:
In central Canada, for example, many transportation services and facilities are highly developed and competitive, with shippers having a choice as to rail, truck, ship or plane. In some parts of Canada, however, while the facilities and services may be well developed, there is a lack of competition ... Still other parts of the country, such as the north, are undeveloped in terms of transportation facilities and services and it is unlikely, in many cases, that there will be much competition because of the nature of the products or the geography over which they move.
Transportation policy must therefore recognize the fact that there is a wide range of facilities and services, operating under different degrees of maturity and competition. It must enable each to be treated in an appropriate manner, and not, as is now the case, as exceptions to a policy which relies principally on competition.
Having made that statement on behalf of the government in June of 1975, we have the Minister of Transport doing everything he can to destroy the whole concept on which the former minister based his statement of June, 1975. This minister is again talking about commercial viability, and instead of a transportation policy which would take into consideration all the modes of transportation which are available in Canada, that is air, rail, bus, ships, and the private motor car, and evolving a policy under which each would be used to the maximum efficiency and at the least cost, we have the minister bringing in a bill to do with the railway, a bill to do with ships, a bill to do with airlines, each one separate, each one devised apparently without thought of what the effects of the proposals would be on the other modes of transportation.
The announcement of transportation policy in June, 1975, included a statement on the responsibility of government to attend to the provision of an efficient total transportation system involving all modes of transport. The Minister of Transport is using a fragmentary approach to transport instead. How can we look at an over-all policy with bits and pieces? By studying the various modes in isolation?
The minister uses the word rationalization a lot. How can we be rational by making cutbacks here and there without eliminating the inefficiencies and waste in the over-all system? For example, this summer there were 56 daily departures of public transport between Montreal and Ottawa, 14 of them commercial aircraft. What about the waste and duplication of having two major airports in Montreal? We have not had a rational discussion about that.
It is not rational to consider operating costs without regard to infrastructure investment. The actual investment in each mode is just as important as subsidization of costs. The implications of transport investment upon employment and energy conservation must also be considered and have never been considered by the government.
Our present transport system does not serve us very well. It is a patchwork of competing modes rather than an integrated complementary system. The result is that we have an unbalanced transport system with congested roads, high energy requirements, and lack of integration between modes.

May 25, 1977
Air Canada
Support for civil aviation infrastructure has grown from $120 million per year in 1954 to $354 million in 1973. Only 25 per cent of infrastructure costs of air travel are covered by charges to the air traveller. The average Canadian does not receive a fair share of this investment benefit. In 1973, 70 per cent of those using air service over long distances had incomes over $10,000, and of these some 65 per cent had incomes in excess of $15,000. The CTC inter-city transport study 1970 found that over 60 per cent of all air trips are made by the segment of society whose income exceeded $13,000 per year. Conversely, the same study found 64 per cent of rail and 73 per cent of bus trips are made by people whose income is less than $11,000 per year.
Yet, federal rail policies have not encouraged growth of rail usage. The hon. member for Dartmouth-Halifax East (Mr. Forrestall) when he spoke earlier talked about the proposal of this government virtually to wipe out rail transportation between St. John's, Newfoundland, and Montreal. Railways are the only mode which attempts to finance all infrastructure out of operating revenue. The type of financing improvement
needed to expand and improve the service has not been provided.
Bus travel has stagnated. No operating subsidies are paid to bus operators. Over 80 per cent of inter-city movement has been by automobile. Road costs have increased from $1 billion in 1955 to $3 billion in 1973. The net loss after revenues was $1.15 billion for roads in Canada in 1973, according to an interim report on inter-city passenger movement in Canada by Transport Canada.
The real costs of transportation must also include costs of accidents, pollution, land use, travel time, and energy usage. Those transport systems such as rail and bus which are most efficient in the use of fuel should receive priority in transport planning. Transport consumes about 25 per cent of all energy in Canada. The minister is quick to tell us that we cannot afford to subsidize rail service and that we must cut back on rail service. Yet the minister continues to increase the subsidies that are given for air travel-
